title: Naming Cartographer, then rebuilding it properly
goal: Put a fuzzy idea into words (a tool that records vibecoding sessions and maps how you build), then make it real: a concept doc and a working /wrap prototype, then a rebuild that is agent-agnostic, language-aware and configurable.
outcome: Named it Cartographer; set solo + teams tiers with the end-of-project replay as the core moment; shipped a v1 prototype in 6 minutes of build time; then rebuilt it as a package with three agent adapters, a prompt-pragmatics layer, aptitude-based config, git-repo projects with branches, auto-wrap hooks, tests and skills.

moves.you: You brain-dumped the idea: a connector that records AI coding sessions and maps how you work over time, and asked for help putting it into words.
moves.prompt: OKAY. i have an app idea, designed for the future of vibecoding. It's a connector to your AI agent that records and analyzes your workflow in the CLI or agent itself… im having trouble aritculating this. help me.
moves.happened: The agent framed it as a flight recorder for vibecoding: git records what changed, chat logs record everything, nothing records how you thought. It proposed that the magic moment was surfacing an old playbook when a new project starts, and closed with three questions: who is it for, private or social, and what is the killer moment.
moves.consequence: The framing stuck and became the product's one-line thesis. The proposed magic moment missed.
moves.response: You stepped away for nineteen minutes, then answered all three questions in one message and corrected the moment.

plain.you: You told the agent your idea in a rush: something that sits next to an AI coding tool, records the session, and shows you how you work over time. You asked for help saying it clearly.
plain.happened: The agent gave it a shape: git keeps what changed, chat logs keep everything, nothing keeps how you thought. It suggested the best moment would be seeing an old playbook when you start something new, and asked three questions: who is it for, private or shared, and what is the one moment that sells it.
plain.consequence: That one-line shape stuck and became the product's pitch. The suggested best moment turned out to be wrong.
plain.response: You went away for nineteen minutes, then answered all three questions in one message and corrected the moment.

moves.you: You made four decisions at once: two editions (solo and teams), social as an option, the killer moment is the end-of-project replay, and the name is Cartographer. You asked for a concept doc and a /wrap prototype.

moves.happened: The agent reordered the whole build around the replay: replay page first, profile later. The name gave the doc and the page one identity.
moves.consequence: One message set the direction for everything that followed, and the agent could start building immediately.
moves.response: You let it look before it built.

moves.you: You asked for a rebuild: agent-agnostic, built for the three most popular coding agents, language-aware prompt pragmatics, retrospective maps, manual or auto wrap, aptitude-based feedback, projects as git repos with branches, and a pricing sketch.
moves.prompt: Rebuild this using Fable. I want the code written advanced enough to capture nuances regardless of the model used to do the coding. Basically, agent agnostic for creating the map but should be built for the three most popular coding agents…
moves.happened: The agent first checked the machine: Python 3.9.6 and only Claude Code history on disk. It set two constraints for itself, write to 3.9 and cover Codex and Cursor with synthetic fixtures, and started.
moves.consequence: Eight capabilities and one quality constraint but no done-condition, so the agent chose the architecture.
moves.response: You raised the effort level and asked for a restart.

moves.you: Still no prompt from you; the agent smoke-tested the generated brief on this session.
moves.happened: Three misreads surfaced: Claude Code writes HEAD as the branch when the folder is not a repo, prompt #3 was read as 'config' because of generic words like 'version', and one test failed because 'make it look nicer… you decide the colors' scored as build.

moves.response: The agent fixed all three: HEAD means no repo, intent matching became stem-tolerant, and ties break away from build. 12 of 12 tests passed.

reusable_prompts.prompt: I have an idea for <thing>. I'm having trouble articulating it. Help me.
reusable_prompts.why: Returns a framing, a structure, pitch variants and the questions that sharpen the idea.

reusable_prompts.prompt: Rebuild <thing> so that it is <property 1>, <property 2>, <property 3>. It must support <A>, <B>, <C>. A <unit of work> is <definition>.
reusable_prompts.why: Batching every requirement into one message let the agent design the architecture once instead of iterating; the cost is that the agent picks the architecture.

patterns: Starts from a messy brain-dump and lets the agent find the words, then corrects the framing.
Steps away to think between framing and deciding (19 min, then 56 min) rather than iterating in chat; comes back with batched decisions.
Makes product decisions fast once shown concrete options: four calls in one message.
Wants both the story (concept doc) and the thing (prototype) at once.
Raises scope sharply after seeing a first version work, and sets quality constraints ('advanced enough to capture nuances') without done-conditions.

time_sinks.what: Thinking pause between pitch and decisions (productive)
Pause between v1 delivery and the rebuild request
Writing the rebuild: adapters, lang, digest, brief, render, hooks, cli, tests

coaching.observation: The rebuild prompt listed eight capabilities but no done-condition, so 'done' was whatever the agent decided to ship.
coaching.suggestion: Add one acceptance line per capability you care most about; it becomes the test list.
coaching.rewrite: Rebuild this as an agent-agnostic package. Done means: (1) `cartographer wrap` works on a Claude Code, Codex and Cursor session, (2) the brief includes a per-prompt reading and language notes, (3) config switches voice and feedback by aptitude, (4) projects are git repos with branches shown in the replay, (5) tests pass on Python 3.9.

coaching.observation: Batching four decisions after a pause worked well: the agent could start building immediately.
coaching.suggestion: Keep doing this; when you batch, also say which item matters most so the agent can order the work.

coaching.observation: The Codex and Cursor adapters are written from format knowledge and synthetic fixtures, not real data.
coaching.suggestion: Before relying on them, run `cartographer sessions --agent codex` on a machine with Codex history and fix whatever the adapter misses; the formats shift between releases.
